utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Skare Ozbolt, I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony still binds you. It seems that we have one technical problem. Meanwhile, we can continue. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to continue your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning Ms. Ozbolt.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yesterday, Ms. Ozbolt, we finished off with you talking about your work down in UN Sector South with various Krajina Serbs that were in that area, encouraging them to stay. And I would like to turn a couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption, Your Honours. I'm not sure that correctly characterizes. I believe the testimony was encouraging those that remained in the UN compound, the families of accused war criminals to stay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was completely a lead-in to go to the next topic, which we were going to. The record of what the witness said speaks for itself. It was merely leading to get to the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes, let's not -- put your next question to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, I would like to show you several forms that were not discussed in your statement but have been part of the supplemental information sheet. Now, I would like to show you two Prosecutor documents. The first one is P56.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could look at that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at this document, Ms. Ozbolt, and I'm going to show you a just small variation, which is P57, and just ask you about both of those. Preliminarily, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's look at P57. How about this document, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't recall this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall documents where Serbs who were -- Krajina Serbs who were leaving the area signed documents saying that they voluntarily wanted to leave the Republic of Croatia. Do you recall that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the time that I was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did sign a form given to them by the UN. However, that was not part, and I didn't pay much attention to it, since on the premises where we talked to these people, there were representatives of UN and quite simply the procedure was first for them to talk to them, then with me, then with the Assistant Minister Penic, and then again with UN representatives. So what they eventually decided was their own decision, and they probably signed something similar to what we see here. But I have to say that I don't remember these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. Did you have any discussions with the UN personnel that were there as to why documents such as -- similar to this might have been signed saying that we wanted to leave Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The UN probably wanted to have some kind of security for themselves because their departure would have been part of the UN procedure of escorting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you talked about Western Slavonia. Did you have any information that the UN or any other international organisation had used a similar form in Western Slavonia after Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they had their own ways of recording the people who wished to leave Croatia, and in doing so, sought assistance from the UN or rather peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift topics with you, and I'd like to talk to you just a little bit about one of the issues that you discussed briefly during your opening comments yesterday. And can you correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe yesterday - and I don't have the final transcript - you noted there were 500.000 Croatian internally displaced people, as well as 300.000 refugees, for a total of approximately 800.000 individuals that the Croatian government was taking care of. And turning to the 800.000, I mean, where were these people being housed by the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever they could. Most of them were accommodated on the sea coast, in the hotels there. Some of them were also placed in hotels inland because there was no other accommodation available. They were also placed in homes or hotels, and those were the people who were forced to leave their own homes. And that was a situation that prevailed since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the individuals that you are saying were forced to leave their homes, are you talking about Croatians that were forced out of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Explain to the Trial Chamber the burden on the Croatian resources that these 800.000 internally displaced people and 300.000 -- excuse me, 500.000 internally displaced people and 300.000 refugees, what kind of burden on Croatian resources these individuals presented?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say, that the 300.000 had come from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the 500.000 were internally displaced persons. They were given accommodation wherever it was possible, primarily in the hotels that were vacant because, quite simply, there was no other way of providing shelter for the people who were flowing in on a daily basis because they were fleeing the terror, and they only had their basic belongings with them. Refugees were arriving in Zagreb almost every day in big columns and convoys, buses, and in any way they could. The only way to provide them with shelter back then in 1991 was in hotels. The refugees who had relatives found shelter with them, but the majority of them sought some kind of security and shelter from the government. If you're asking me about the burden, that was a tremendous burden because, in that way, Croatia had to make available all its tourist resources, meaning hotels, bungalows, holiday resorts, et cetera, which meant that there was no tourism; and, of course, as part of the economy it died down completely. People were, of course, jobless. Somebody had to provide support for them, and throughout all these years, that was an enormous cost and burden on the budget and on the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us talk for a moment about the Croats who were displaced from the Krajina. And the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that numerous Croatian homes in the Krajina were destroyed between 1991 and 1995. And you have talked about the peaceful reintegration policy and a part of that policy was bringing displaced Croats back to the areas that they were displaced from. Now, during this period of time, however, the attempt was to bring displaced people back to an area where their homes were, in fact -- had been destroyed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were attempts to return them, and the goal was to restore the ratio of the population that had existed in 1991, before the expulsion and before the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, post Operation Storm, you and the other officials in the president's office -- did you?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I think counsel got the message which was to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I didn't get any message at all. You stood up in the middle of my question, so I figured I would stop and let you have your say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's first calm down, yes? I come back to the first time Ms. Gustafson intervened. I let it go, but of course she was right. You misrepresented what was said yesterday that was talking with the family - -

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of those who had remained and not what you told the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was merely a lead-in to what we were going into those documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not only leading, it was leading not -- it was leading not accurately representing where you left off yesterday. I let it go at the time. Ms. Gustafson, at the same time, is well aware, I take it, Ms. Gustafson, that going into details which do not really affect matters should be limited to the necessary. Let's continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, did you and other members in the president's office, and this is after Storm, did you receive information about burning and looting going on in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that, Ms. Ozbolt?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reaction was extremely negative. I was personally ashamed of such a conduct. It was not only shameful, but we demanded that the perpetrators be found and punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you or did you have -- in addition to you, did you or any of the people that you talked to in the president's office, had you expected and planned for that type of conduct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that such conduct was truly unexpected. We had launched Operation Flash, that was conducted in an extremely good manner, and it did not end up in such situations. And I must say that nobody within the government had expected to see what took place after Operation Storm. I talked about this with the president. He was rather upset and angry because of that. He even told me at one point that this was actually a sabotage, because his efforts had been aimed, and I think that was also a promise given to everyone that the military operation would be completed swiftly and that we would proceed towards the continuation of the process of reintegration. Therefore, this kind of conduct was completely unexpected, horrendous and it blemished the overall efforts made by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, when you were working as the assistant Chief of Staff, did you ever see any actions by President Tudjman that indicated to you that there either was a plan to burn and loot property in the Krajina or to allow people to burn and loot property in the Krajina after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when this happened, did the looting and the burning of Serb homes, did that complicate or make difficult the re-sheltering of Croatian internally displaced people who might have wanted to come back to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just an interruption. Again, I'd like to ask that these questions be asked in a non-leading way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, was it leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was, Mr. Kehoe. Please reformulate your question in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it looting and burning complicate the plans for the Republic of Croatia, as it went to reintegration?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still leading, Mr. Kehoe. You could ask what the effect was of the looting and burning on the development and implementation of policy matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Taking His Honour's question and I re-ask it, hopefully, in the same fashion that His Honour Judge Orie did. What was the effect of the looting and burning on the development and implementation of the policy matters for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had an adverse effect. No one in the government, in their right mind, would condone the burning and the looting. The president discussed this matter with the representatives and ambassadors from the contact group. Also, this was done by the prime minister, the minister of foreign affairs, the minister of the interior; but no one had expected that that would occur. I have to say that the reaction of all the parties who were involved in this and who were in the leadership of the country, they were shocked. Nobody stood to defend those who were involved in burning and looting, and there were requests for them to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the number of the people prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Interpreters could not hear the number you apparently mentioned. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, what impact, if any, did this burning and looting have on housing of Croatian internally displaced people?

It was extremely foolhardy to set houses on fire, because, for those people who were supposed to come back, it was difficult to find accommodation precisely due to the burning. In addition, it created confusion and difficulties, not to mention the shame that we all felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what difficulties, if any, it presented to the Republic of Croatia on the international political level?

At the time when Operation Storm was in the planning phase, I said that we wanted to find a peaceful solution to the very end. However, since this was rejected by Martic's government, a military operation was launched with the intention of conducting it for a very short period of time, and that it would be followed by as quick restoration of normal life as possible. That was our plan. Therefore, there was no plan to go into looting or setting fire on houses following Operation Storm, because it was totally unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question for you is that the impact on the Republic of Croatia, the impact or difficulty it presented to the Republic of Croatia on the international political level.
It was an adverse impact because nobody would condone looting and burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me move on -- we have talked about this property destruction issue and then I want to address one last issue with you concerning the temporary takeover of property. Are you familiar with the law in the Republic of Croatia on the temporary takeover of property?
Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now -- and I want you to, in your answer to explain your -- your -- in your testimony with respect to confiscation and sequestration, did this law allow the Croatian government to confiscate property that was abandoned by the Krajina Serbs who had left the area? Did it allow that?

Oftentimes, especially representatives of the government and minister for the reconstruction and development had, as their task, the need to explain that the law at no cost allowed the confiscation of property because private property is protected in Croatia under the law. Following Operation Storm, as well as Operation Flash, certain individuals decided to leave the Republic of Croatia, and, in doing so, left their property behind, precisely in order to make sure that the properties did not remain deserted and thus open to possible attempts at looting or burning; and while, at the same time, we had large numbers of refugees whose accommodation in hotels became untenable. The government enacted this sort of law which was of temporary character - and I highlight it was of temporary character - whereby these refugees would be put up on a temporary basis in such abandoned homes. And the refugees to be given that accommodation largely came from Bosnia-Herzegovina, although some were from Croatia as well, until such time as their homes were reconstructed or rebuilt, or until such time as the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina would be able to go back to their homes in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this law, was there a requirement that Serbs who left -- was there a requirement that those individuals sell that property to the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Once again, I object to the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, isn't a -- aren't you leading to whether or not selling was an issue. Could you ask it in such a way that, whether there were any requirements, if you would leave the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning our attention to this property and potential sales of this property, were there any requirements concerning that sale?

The question includes the term "requirement." There was no such requirement. There was a possibility for those who did not wish to return to Croatia to sell their property, either on the market or to the Government of Croatia. In agreement with representatives of the international community, an agency was set up for the sale of real estate, which sold and bought such properties, or, better put, it bought such properties off. Such an agency was also set up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I believe the same was true for Serbia. It was meant for all those individuals who no longer wished to live in their earlier or previous places of residence. In this way, the Government of the Republic of Croatia bought a good many such properties. It bought the properties by paying up money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you, Mr. Ozbolt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kay, do you have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find out whether you will examine or cross-examination her. Ms. Ozbolt, you will now be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I really apologise for the interruption. I just want to inform the Court that we're having technical difficulties. The compter here is dead. We're not able to release our cross-examination documents. At the moment, we're working on it, and we'll get them as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you need the assistance of any technicians then please inform the Registry so that they can assist you. Mr. Kay, are you not bothered by the lack of computer assistance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is probably a help rather than a hindrance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ms. Ozbolt, we know that Operation Storm started on the 4th of August of 1995. When did you first know that that military operation was going to take place?

It's a difficult question, requiring a very specific answer. Since, throughout that time, I was within the chain -- the flow of communication, we knew that an operation would ensue should the negotiations in Geneva fail. If you're asking me if I knew of it, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so there came a moment, did there, when information came to you that the military operation was -- was going to go forward. Would that have been the day before the 4th of August, something like that?
Yes. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that then certain plans involving military, Ministry of Interior, other government agencies, started going forward from that date?
Probably. Although I was not privy to these plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to Mr. Cermak, would it be right to say that before the 4th of August and Operation Storm started, that his name and he had not featured in any of that flow of information concerning the operation?
No, it did not. He was not mentioned. He was a businessman at the time, deeply immersed in his business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just looking at him during that period, as you've described him, a businessman, would it be right to say that for a couple of years he had been outside political life. He hadn't been involved in politics?

The last time he engaged in politics, was, I believe, as a minister of energy and industry. So he was a member of the government, charged with energy industry, and ship-building industry, I believe. This was some time in 1993, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We know that he was appointed by President Tudjman on the 5th of August to be the garrison commander of -- of Knin. When did you first hear that General Cermak was being considered for a position in relation to Knin?

Well, roughly at that same time. The idea was, as I've already said, to bring the military operation to its end as soon as possible and to start restoring the communications system and to revitalise the entire area. The president wanted to find an adequate person for the job. He was looking for a businessman of the sort who would be able to have the entire matter up and running quite soon, and his choice was Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say, then, that at that time, the idea came about that something would have to be done in relation to Knin, if it was liberated, to enable its reintegration and reconstruction inside Croatia?

I think that I said yesterday that the Croatian government felt that it was in dire straits when it came to the economic situation and that the situation was untenable. The military situation was a condition sine qua non, however it had to be done with as soon as possible in order to start revitalising the economy and life in general. However, there was a great deal to be done there since the Republic of Serbian Krajina was in total disarray. The only structure working there at the time was the military. The schools, the health system, and the economy, the latter, practically non-existent, did not function at all. The southern parts of Croatia were cut off from the mainland, which posed a serious economic problem. The third problem were refugees whom the government could no longer sustain under the circumstances. All of these matters called for a swift action. It was necessary to start revitalising the entire country as soon as possible. That was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it known then that since 1991, when the Republika Srpska Krajina established itself in Knin and the surrounding area, that there had been no investment, no development, no going forward in terms of living conditions?

Yes, correct. Nobody would invest in a -- a war-affected area of high risk. Croatia was designated a war zone. This was definitely an enormous problem of the tourists stayed away, investors steered clear of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that there was the government's trustee for Knin, a man called Mr. Petar Pasic. Were you familiar with his name and his position?

Yes. By virtue of its authority, the government appointed commissioners or trustees to such areas who were supposed to be constantly in touch with the government and carry out all the decisions issued by the government and addressing the relevant areas covered by commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would those responsibilities have been involving the government's trustee, providing conditions to ensure an economic revival, getting the town working, and the normalisation of life in Knin? Would that have been one of the responsibilities and tasks of such a person?
Yes. That would have been the responsibility of such a person. Although, the problems prevalent in Knin went far beyond the abilities and possibilities vested with Pasic as a trustee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that one of the purposes of sending Mr. Cermak to Knin would have been for him to help support and work with Mr. Pasic in his tasks?

Mr. Pasic was a government official. Mr. Cermak was an erstwhile minister, a retired general, and a businessman. He had very high organisation skills. The idea and the message behind Cermak's appointment to Knin was to place emphasis on reconstruction, economic revival, restoration of communication, and, in general, normalisation of life. If you will allow me to continue, we had a similar situation in Western Slavonia, where, in addition to the trustee, other individuals were appointed there as coordinators, as it were, who could assist in the whole process. The same idea was applied to the Knin area. However, these same individuals who were engaged in Western Slavonia could simply not be spared from Western Slavonia in order for them to be dispatch to the south because there remained a great deal of work to be done in Western Slavonia. Thus, Cermak was the choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that he was also known as someone who was an expert in logistics and organisation of projects from his experiences of working as a minister from 1991 until 1993?

As I said, he was known to be a rather good organiser. Since he covered a field which was largely that of the economy, he was the ideal person for the job. He also had that military background of generalship behind him, and, to put it simply, it was a good combination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that in making this appointment, there was no intention of President Tudjman to make Mr. Cermak the commander of the police, the civil police in the region?

You see, if President Tudjman wanted to appoint a civilian policeman, he would have done so. The emphasis was placed on the need for an individual to be appointed to that job who could bring about the normalisation of life there. There were no intentions of introducing any sort of a military regime, particularly in view of the delicate situation that obtained there, and in view of the fact that the message that had been sent across to the population there had, throughout that time been, We want you to remain here and be integrated into the Croatian system. The appointment of a military person or a policeman of any sort would have come across as some sort of duress or oppression, which was not the goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say, then, that President Tudjman did not send Mr. Cermak down there to be in command of a military regime of the area.
Yes. That was not his objective; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know from evidence in the case that the international community were based in an UNCRO camp in Knin, and that at the time of the liberation of Knin, a large number of the Serbian and Croatian population had gathered in that place. Did that event cause any problems, so far as you know, in relation to the plan and strategy of the government, or the president, for that matter?

If you can be more specific in your question as to what sort of problem it could pose. There were several hundred individuals in that camp who found shelter in the UN camp. The UN requested our assistance in the resolution of the situation, which we provided. That was the first time I went to Knin. General Cermak was there. I think we went to the camp together. I stayed behind, and he left, returning thereafter perhaps, I don't remember. We resolved the situation, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've told us that Mr. Cermak's job was the normalisation of life. Was he also given the task of liaising, on behalf of the Croatian government, with the UNCRO commander and internationals based at that camp?

Look, at this moment, I can really not give you specifics what his powers were. Unfortunately, what we -- or, rather, the president entrusted Mr. Cermak with, such a model does not exist anywhere in the world. If you're asking me about his powers, he was, in a way, a landless knight; I would put it that way. He held a position of a coordinator and the area of his competence was unknown. If you're asking me about liaising with UNCRO representatives, he to communicate with him. Somebody had to go there and solve those problems. Whether that was within his powers or not, he was quite simply forced to solve the problems that they came up with to him on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it ever predicted that the UNCRO camp in Knin would present itself as a problem for the future planning of what was to happen in Knin?
Can you please clarify the question? I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it predicted in those days of the 4th/5th of August, that the relationships with UNCRO and the people in the camp was something that would present a problem as between the UN and Croatia?
No. The problem arose when the UN said that those people refused to leave the camp and that that was creating logistical problems for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that the Croatian side - the Croatian government and its organisations - viewed this area as being their sovereign territory that they had liberated, belonging to them --
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and that the internationals, now on their territory, were not there with the same authority that they had previously had, and with the same role?

Well, the UN authority remained unchanged. However, Croatia restored its authorities there, and the UN was there to assist this process. I would put it this way: Something that should have been done under the auspices of UN, and later UNCRO, was actually achieved by the government itself. Let me remind you that the goal of the UN peacekeeping mission was not only to stop the war but also to effect demilitarisation and launch the restoration of normal life, which involved the return of refugees and revival of the whole area. These were the UN tasks, according to the UN resolutions. However, since this did not happen, Croatia introduced its authority on its own, but the UN remained there and helped the things being put in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go now to an exhibit in the case. It's Exhibit D28. And it's the agreement that was signed between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Sarinic on the 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just produce that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that, Ms. Ozbolt?
Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is this a document that you're familiar with?
Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware of it being signed at the time by Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see what the terms of the agreement concern. And in relation to particular issues, we know that, under paragraph 3, that there is an section which, "Croatia encourages all those previous inhabitants of the Republic of Croatia ... who so wish to remain peacefully in the areas over which Croatian authority is exercised." Croatia will allow full guarantees for security, the departure of those who don't want to stay in Croatia, except those who committed violation of international criminal law. And in the event of any such departures, Croatia was to allow UNCRO and other organisations and assist and coordinate in departures from -- from the region. Are you able to help us with a little bit of the background concerning this document and this paragraph in particular?

Therefore, anyone who wished to leave Croatia within the organisation and under supervision of UNCRO would apply to them. They would probably have to fill out a form that we had seen earlier today, and they would be escorted out of Croatia by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In making this agreement, Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi, were they both aware at the time that because these --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like that ask for foundation to be made as to the knowledge of the state of mind of Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you follow that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can, and I accept it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know why -- well, you have answered that already. Well, I'll ask this again. Do you know why this paragraph was inserted into the agreement by both parties?
Because particularly some of the people who were in the camp that we mentioned before actually wanted to leave Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This agreement applies to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I'm not sure that foundation was really laid by that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we haven't heard the follow-up question, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm -- I must say I'm at a loss to know why we're getting these objections because this is obviously a key issue in the case and involves the anticipated departure of people from the Croatian territory as envisaged by Mr. Akashi on behalf of the United Nations. We know that he was the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, and Mr. Sarinic, who was the advisor to President Tudjman and head of his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed with your line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see that this document applies to Sector North and Sector South. How much information was there at the time that you were aware of of the scale of people who wanted to leave Croatia at that time?

I have to say that I was not aware of the number of the people who wished to leave Croatia. Akashi visited our office and told us that there were some people who didn't want to live in Croatia any longer. It was agreed on that occasion that their departure would be coordinated with the UN. And, for that reason, we have this clause in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the issue, then, of those who had committed crimes, did you -- are you able to inform the Court as to what you knew about that issue and why it was asserted inside this agreement?

A provision was inserted in this agreement for those who want -- were allowed to leave, with the exception of those who were in breach of international criminal law, i.e., those who had committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what preparations the Croatian government was taking at that time to deal with any such suspects or people accused of war crimes who they believed were part of that population who might want to leave Croatia? Do you know what steps were being taken to deal with that issue? The Court is aware of the background concerning events in 1991 and onwards, in general terms.

Those who had committed crimes in the areas of Sector South and Sector North were identified. Their names were known. The witnesses who had fled the area, or were expelled from it, testified to that in court. There were trials conducted against the people who were believed to have committed war crimes. Their names, the events, and the witnesses were known to the courts, and it was the courts who had them on their wanted lists. And precisely for that reason, of their being on either the wanted lists or because they were already subject to legal proceedings, or, if they were already convicted in absentia, is the reason for this provision to be included in this agreement, meaning that these people had to be brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was this a matter, then, at that time that was with the Ministry of Justice?
The Ministry of Justice was only a body that transmitted the request that came either from the state prosecutor or directly from the courts, and they conveyed these requests to UNCRO at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So there were lists of -- of suspects, is that right, who were people who had been named before the Croatian justice system. Is that the situation at that time?
Yes. The Ministry of Justice had a list of people that were sought by the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you would allow me to seek some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were talking about persons tried in absentia, so, therefore, convicted persons. When Mr. Kay asked you a follow-up question, he asked you whether there, therefore, were lists of suspects. Of course, suspects and convicted persons is not the same. And in your answer you said, "The Ministry of Justice had a list of people that were sought by the judiciary." Now that could be both, I take it, accused and those already convicted. Could you give us an impression about the number of persons that were convicted for war crimes? As I understand from you, most of them would be tried in absentia. But could you give us the impression of the number of people that were tried already for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the list that the ministry had were the lists of people who were in different stages of prosecution or proceedings and that were wanted. Those who were convicted were given a possibility, given that they had been tried and convicted in absentia, to be retried. I cannot recall exactly at the moment how many of those were on the list of the people against whom final judgements were passed, but I think there were about 40-ish people or there about. I cannot give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something like that. For the Krajina only or in Sector North or south?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krajina only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Krajina only. Now, how long was the list of those who were suspected and, therefore, sought by the prosecutorial services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lists of suspects was quite a long one, and it encompassed the whole country. It consisted of over 400 names of the people who were wanted on suspicion that had -- they had perpetrated crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Crimes or war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the exception says international criminal law. That's, of course, not every crime. Would that -- may I make the question more specific. Would that include being a member of an armed force, which was an illegal armed force? That is to say, that it occupied the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This does not include participation in an armed rebellion or possession of weapons, because amnesty was declared for these kind of felonies on four occasions throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, a correction must be made because Your Honour is dealing with matters. It was 4.000 not 400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Then I either misunderstood or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a mistranslation as I am instructed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- you said 4.000 the long list of suspects? Yes. That is it then now clear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I come back to my question. You said this included crime, not necessarily war crimes. Is that -- I asked you crimes or war crimes. Your answer was crimes. Do you know how many of them were suspected of having committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I honestly don't know the exact number. This list that contained over 4.000 names included those who committed murders that were not qualified as war crimes. Therefore, this number did not include minor criminal offences but, rather, really serious crimes or a suspicion of serious crimes. How many of them were actually accused of war crimes is difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we look at a document now, Exhibit P388. It's a letter dated the 8th of August, 1995, sent by General Cermak to General Forand, and so two days after the Akashi/Sarinic agreement. And if we just have a look at this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Cermak was asking for a list of the refugees in the camp so that he could address their problems and see that passes are issued to all who want to leave the camp and go on living in the area of Knin. Just looking at that, was there an issue that those people who had been in the RSK and were now under Croatian sovereignty were required to have some sort of identification papers and to register as Croatian nationals, if they were to be Croatian citizens?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The letter says we will provide conditions of normal life for them together with UNCRO, draw up a list of women, children, and persons older than 60 who may leave the camp unimpededly; and if they do not wish to return to the liberated areas, but want transport to Bosnia or Serbia, we shall provide that as well. And then the next paragraph: It is necessary to make a list of men aged between 18 and 60 who will have to be interviewed by the representatives of the civilian police of the Republic of Croatia, in cooperation with your people. They will be provided with health care, access by the Red Cross, and other humanitarian organisations. All those who have not committed any crimes against the Republic of Croatia will be allowed to go back to Knin, while those who do not want this will be given transport to Bosnia or Serbia. Those detained will be handed to the judicial authorities of the Republic of Croatia. Please could you give me this list at once so that we can together settle the problems that have arisen. Having seen that letter now, have you ever seen that letter before?
It is possible that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All right. It's --
I'm sorry, it's been a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just the issues in the letter, and --
Well, that was the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at that paragraph about the list of the men whom General Cermak said were to be interviewed by the civilian police as well as the international people, and then the issue of any crimes, that any may have been committed; this letter written by General Cermak, do you know if that was a measure taken by him acting on behalf of the Ministry of Justice, in relation to this matter?
Well, that was probably requested of him by the Ministry of Justice, since the Ministry of Justice was in possession of the names of people who were wanted by the judiciary and the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it the case, then, that Croatia wanted to sort this matter out quickly in relation to any suspects or any who may have been convicted who were inside the UNCRO camp taking shelter?
Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You, as we've seen from the papers, were eventually dealing with this matter with an assistant minister for justice, a Mr. Tomislav Penic; is that right?

I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand. Yes, yes. I did not discuss this issue with Mr. Tomislav Penic. We came across this issue in the president's office when Mr. Akashi drew our attention to it. It seemed difficult to solve the problem and, at that point, we got involved in that. Ultimately, I went down to the camp, together with Mr. Penic. We talked to the families of these individuals and provided them assurances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just cut you short there as we will be going into that a little bit later on. And it is just one last question which will then be appropriate for the break, with Your Honours' leave. Had Mr. Penic been dealing with this matter before you on behalf of the Ministry of Justice and as it became more and more of a problem between the UN and Croatia, you, from the president's office, were brought in?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you give us an indication of how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will probably need only 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate needing quite a bit of time in cross. Approximately four to five hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I write everything down. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the time needed by the parties. The Chamber is of the opinion that it should be possible to finish the testimony of this witness this week. That is, today and tomorrow. For those purposes, Mr. Kay, you asked for another two hours. You'll have that next session even if that would be a bit of an extended session, which gives you one hour, 35; one hour, 40, approximately. Try to squeeze in your question. Then, Mr. Mikulicic, you get the 15 minutes that you ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. If I could be of any assistance, in the meantime I rescheduled, and I'll have no questions on that witness. So my 15 minutes is on disposal to other Defences and to the Prosecution office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I suggest that you take a relatively long session with the assistance of interpreters and transcriber but certainly not more than one hour and 45 minutes. Then, Ms. Gustafson would you have the remaining time this morning and two sessions tomorrow, which brings you to approximately three and a half hours then. A little bit over three and a half hours. We would then have the third session for tomorrow for Judges's questions and re-examination. That is the schedule on which we will work, which I may also make clear to you, Ms. Ozbolt, that we expect to finish tomorrow at a quarter to 2.00. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just checking the clock and see if I can beat the clock. I'll skip a few documents then. Let's turn to 65 ter 1D2614.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document that just in English, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, but that I believe you're able to read English because I think you will recognise some -- the document. This has not been translated into Croatian, Your Honour. It is not a language of the Tribunal as Your Honour knows, so it is just the English document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If all the Defence teams and accused agree with having it only available in English, then, of course, we can proceed. If not, then, of course, we would insist on having a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We certainly agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We agree as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Ms. Skare Ozbolt? It's addressed to you on the 2nd of September, 1995?
Yes, I do recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see some handwriting on the document. Is that your handwriting?
No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know whose handwriting that is?
I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just look at the content of the letter, it's from Mr. Harston of the United Nations, and he had spoken to you the day before, and we see that he is recommending agreement with regard to the displaced people in the UN compound. And he says that charges and supporting evidence for 62 persons should be made available, that there should be a meeting to discuss each case on an individual basis. On the basis of those discussions, the UN will be prepared to release those listed to the Croatian authorities, and then he puts a number of conditions. We see the words "okay" written down the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2. I won't go through all the detail. To ensure proper identification of individuals, and if there is any disagreement on the conditions that it should be referred to the ICTY. And then he makes suggestions concerning the immediate departure for those who are not among the 62 listed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, then, looking at this letter from Mr. Harston, were there problems in the way that he had addressed this issue on behalf of the UN, as far as the Government of Croatia was concerned?
I think that is an answer to this letter of Mr. Harston's that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is. Would you like to turn to that now?
It wouldn't be a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be entered into evidence. There is an version, I believe, of it already, but without the handwriting on. And Your Honour may recollect we had this similar issue yesterday with a previously presented document. The handwriting might actually be informative of the issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although if we do not know who wrote it, then it hardly adds that it appears that one person on this world seems to be okay with some matters. And someone is struggling apparently with what a summons and what an indictment is. But what does it add, Mr. Kay, to our knowledge? Or does it add to confusion on who that one person might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it shows that there was an issue within the Government of Croatia as to what was being asked by United Nations. Your Honour knows that there is a criticism from the Croatian side about the lack of comprehension of the Croatian system by the international lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, then, this and that's the underlying suggestion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or assumption, that this is a copy of the letter which is found within Croatian government circles --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not coming from any other source. Is that how I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because then it makes sense what you say. If we do not have such an assumption, then it could have been any legal clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're not sure. I obtained this copy from Mr. Harston's statement disclosed in the proceedings. That's why it is marked JH/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any observation as far as admission into evidence is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar the number for this document would be ... There appear to be too many microphones open. Could ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1479.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. The Chamber would appreciate receiving information as to where this document originates from, not who drafted it, but where this copy with this handwriting was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll look into it at the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D634, which is the letter you were referring to, Ms. Ozbolt. It is dated the 4th of September, 1995, written by you and about the draft UNCRO agreement. It was sent to you, sorry. Got my documents misplaced. Sent to you. And it concerns information from a professor Vukas and Muljacic, an assistant minister in the foreign ministry. And it's about the draft UNCRO agreement, and this legal opinion was sent to you. Is that right? Did you receive this document?
Yes, I did. And I recognise it. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could I assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the interpretation had problems with the expansion SOFA. SOFA is a brief for a status of forces agreement, as far as I'm aware of from my legal background. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the issue being dealt with by you, was there not only conflict concerning the system of Croatian law versus any other form of law, as well as the issue of validity in international law, concerning rights and obligations in dealing with these people?

That's correct. I told Mr. Harston that we would be absolutely adhering to all the provisions of international law. However, Mr. Harston had only just arrived and was not familiar with the subject matter he was charged with, which created a certain degree of nervousness both on our side and in Mr. Akashi's office. Due to his lack of adequate knowledge, the whole process lasts longer than it should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was eventually another letter written to you on the 9th of September, Exhibit D637. I won't look at that. But to save time, we'll look at a letter with you that you wrote, Exhibit D638, as the Court is familiar with the background, having seen these documents before. And let us skip a stage and go to the letter written by you, Exhibit D638. This was a letter written on the 11th of September?
That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you refer to a letter of the 9th of September. And, again, it concerns issues of the protocol that was to be applied as between the UN and the Croatian authorities for dealing with these people whom the Croatian justice system wanted to deal with. We can see an explanation in paragraph 3, the issue of a charge sheet and decision on the conduct of an investigation, and the point that a charge sheet is issued only after an investigation has been carried out. And the rest of the terms of the letter can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we quickly turn to page 2, to enable the Court to familiarise itself again with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that this was a conflict of legal cultures taking place between Croatia and Mr. Harston and the people he represented?

That's how it could be put, indeed. It was a conflict of legal cultures, but it extended only to Mr. Harston. Other members of Mr. Akashi's team from his legal department assisted me in assuring Mr. Harston of the substance of the Criminal Code of Croatia and the Law on Criminal Procedure of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we look, then, at another document, 2D15-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it is from Mr. Penic, whom you told us about at the Ministry of Justice. A letter to you dated the 11th of September, 1995. If we look, first of all, at the front page and we see the message: "I understood this is important. If you want to know more, please call."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He refers to a memo of the UN from the 9th of September, 1995. That's Exhibit D637; we've no need to look at but to link. And there is an explanation there of the system to be applied within the Croatian criminal justice system, as regards the investigation against 35 suspects. Do you recognise this document as the document being sent to you?
I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the next page, page 3, so that everyone has had a chance to see that page, again, the details on there, signed by Mr. Penic. And is this document, then, an explanation as to what was required to be in conformity with the Croatian criminal justice system and the way that the system would operate?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1480.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to what was happening, this was being played out at the level in Zagreb, the government level, with the United Nations headquarters; is that right?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to Mr. Cermak's involvement, as we know from other evidence, he was presenting statements and discussing the matter with Mr. -- General Forand. Would it be right to say that he was there acting as a channel on behalf of the Croatian government?

Yes. He was a coordinator of sorts. All the information that had to be dealt with locally with UNCRO, with General Forand, that -- for that information, it was General Cermak who was the point of contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Eventually this matter was solved, and the procedure followed to enable these suspects or people charged to go into the criminal justice system. Were there also other representatives of the Croatian government involved? Slobodan Lang, do you know him, and was he also involved in this process?

Yes. Slobodan Lang was advisor to the president for humanitarian issues. He was frequently present in the areas where human rights needed protecting. He accompanied me on my trips very often. In the course of autumn and particularly winter of 1995 on to 1996, he travelled the areas in the capacity of advisor to the president on a fact-finding mission and in order to report on the situation in the field with regard to the protection of human rights. He launched a campaign called Let's Save Lives, which was meant to protect the elderly who lived in the mountainous area of the Glina and Knin regions who needed a supply of firewood, foodstuffs and medication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to another document now. Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm just checking whether I have done my housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In the meantime, I can inform the Court that D1479 was provided to the OTP by Mr. Harston in March 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we look now at a document 2D15-0043.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's a letter dated 22nd of September, 1995, from you to Mr. Pitkanen, head of political and humanitarian affairs of UNCRO Zagreb. And it is a response from the Ministry of Justice regarding the UNCRO request for the monitoring of legal proceedings. And do you recognise this document as being one sent by you?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see there what was written by Mr. Penic on the 21st of September and sent to you concerning the monitoring of legal proceedings by UNCRO and his explanation there. Would it be right to say that you were being used as a channel yourself now, in dealing with the specifics of this matter as between UNCRO and the Ministry of Justice.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1481.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn now to D15-0049.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This, again, is another document from Mr. Penic to you. It's got a date on the fax of 16th of October, 1995. Right, I can see we've got the order of the document now. It's the second page. But it's a document dated 2nd of October, and it concerns the monitoring of judicial proceedings. We can see the content of the letter there, and it concerns monitoring. If we turn to page 2, we can see it was sent by Mr. Penic, and we can see the terms of the letter about the requests and cooperation and collaboration. Do you recognise this document as being sent to you by Mr. Penic?

That's correct. We warmly welcomed the UNCRO initiative to follow court proceedings. We thought that was a very good thing to do. The trials were public, and it was a positive development that observers should be following trials and court proceedings in general. The whole initiative went through my office and the Ministry of Justice, since none of the international representatives were able to communicate directly with the Croatian judiciary. It so happened, therefore, that the Ministry of Justice sent a letter to the president of the Supreme Court, and to the presidents of the courts seized of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just turn, then, to page 3 of the document in e-court where we can see a note by Mr. Penic to that effect, which I turn to without anything any question, but just so that the Court can see the document and the context of the witness's evidence, if that meets with the Court's approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe this document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1482.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it is perhaps due to our own scheduling. This monitoring possibility, was that -- and I think it was in one of the documents we have seen but went rather quickly. Was that limited to public hearings or was it also non-public hearings? Perhaps the witness could tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hearings were followed regardless of the fact whether the Court decided that they should be public or closed for public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So monitoring possibilities were there also for non-public hearings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's all I ask you about on this matter. Thank you. The next matter I want to ask you questions about concern the police officer, Mr. Ivkanec. And if we could just look at a document, first of all. 2D15-0063.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour will see reference to this evidence in paragraph 3 of the witness's 65 ter statement, and paragraph 10, for the Court's reference. 2D15-0063.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 17th of September, 1992. And it's the decision by the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, to appoint temporarily Mr. Ivkanec to the Bjelovar police administration in the position of commander of Pakrac police station. And can you see that the appointment was made effective from 18th of September at 1992. And, is that right, that, at the time of Operation Flash, Mr. Ivkanec was within the Ministry of Interior as a policeman and commander of Pakrac police station?

This is the first time that I see this decision. It is an internal document issued by the Ministry of Interior. Therefore, I can only confirm that that was probably the case, since this looks like a genuine decision. Mr. Ivkanec, as far as I know, after Operation Flash, was in charge of restoring safety and security in Eastern [as interpreted] Slavonia. And as far as I remember, he was a suitable person to do that because he had good relationships with representatives of the Serbs, Veljko Dzakula, in particular, at the time and also before Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Something has been pointed on the transcript. That is should be Western Slavonia or Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm grateful for that, and it was going to form my next question actually because we will go to a document now, 2D15-0061. As you told us, you were involved in Eastern Slavonia much later --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- than 1999. Let's go to this document now, 2D15-0061. It's dated 6th of May, 1995. Can you tell us, first of all, when Operation Flash started an ended?
[Interpretation] Operation Flash started on the 1st of January [as interpreted]at 5.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: January or May?
1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see that this is dated the 6th of May, 1995. It's a document signed by -- it says representative Colonel General Cervenko, and if could you just look at the detail of the document as we go through it. It is sent to the Bjelovar Military District, and it says with the aim of organising and coordinating activities in order to accommodate prisoners from Western Slavonia to search the terrain, ensure life conditions for civilians, the coordination staff is established and formed by the president of the Republic of Croatia and made up by the following people: Number 1, Major-General Mate Lausic, for the work and duties of the military police; number 2, Josko Moric, department minister of the interior for the work and tasks which are carried out by the Ministry of Interior, personnel and units; and Ivan Majdak, on behalf of the government, for dealing with work and tasks under the jurisdiction of the government and for the work, coordination of planning and carrying out tasks of the Croatian Army commands and units, in cooperation with MUP units, civil protection, military police in Western Slavonia, on behalf of the Main Staff; Brigadier Luka Dzanko, commander of the Bjelovar Military District was obligated to implement regulated and ordered measures and activities regarding the cooperation and participation with other parties in the area of Western Slavonia. First of all, have you seen this document before?
No, I haven't. But I am aware of the content of the decision and I know that these people were charged with these tasks. But, as I said, I have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it right that what the document was establishing after Operation Flash that the responsibility for the work and duties of the military police would be within the coordination staff under General Lausic?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to the work of the civil police, again, the possibility being under Josko Moric?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Dr. Majdak -- I said Dr. Majdak. Ivan Majdak is a doctor. Dr. Majdak, isn't he?
Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Majdak. If you could explain to the Court what exactly his job was at that time in May 1995?

Roughly speaking, Ivan Majdak's job could be equated or reflected on what was supposed to be done by Mr. Cermak. Namely, Ivan Majdak was an advisor to the president of the Republic in 1990 and 1991. He was then advisor for the economy. After that, he was the minister of agriculture in the Government of the Republic of Croatia. At the time when he assumed these duty, I think that he was also a private entrepreneur and businessman at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. -- or Dr. Majdak, was he, in fact, the superior of Mr. Pasic, the government trustee, and the line to which Mr. Pasic reported to in Knin?

He was not appointed the government's commissioner. There's a substantial difference there. He was a -- the coordinator for economic affairs, involving the normalisation of life. So something similar to what Mr. Cermak was supposed to do in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1484.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just moving now to Knin from that snapshot there of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to P515.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 3rd of August, 1995. And it's a record from the military police administration before Operation Storm on a meeting between the heads of the MUP, military police administration, and SIS, 3rd of August; and was on the subject of harmonising the work of the MUP, military police, and SIS in the preparation and during planned offensives operations by Croatian Army in the forthcoming period. And we can see who was present there: Assistant minister, Mr. Moric; chief of police, Mr. Djurica. Just looking at him there and his name, is it correct that he became the senior coordinator, in relation to the civilian police in Knin and the region after the liberation of Knin?

I think that was the case. Although I have to admit, I wasn't involved any longer in the issues relating to Knin because I became engaged in the issues relating to Eastern Slavonia, so I cannot tell you what the situation was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just look at this document, as it -- it concerns the coordination between the military police and the civilian police. And if we look at page 2. As the text shows, the names of the people present. Court is familiar with some of these names from various documents. I won't repeat them. But it was -- the meeting was opened by Mr. Moric, who outlined a key point: "Yesterday's meeting," so on the 2nd of August, "between the minister of defence and minister of the interior, basic principles confirmed for the operations of the police and military police in wartime conditionals, which were based on experiences in Western Slavonia." And he and General Lausic were aware of negative experiences and it was there joint task to eliminate those problems and ensure full cooperation and performance of tasks. Page 3: The MUP had undertake structural and other preparations for the forthcoming tasks and raised issues with the police administrations. And that they had noticed in Western Slavonia the problem of the activities of irregulars, persons who had not participated in combat operations appeared near the lines in HV uniforms. Court can see that they were dispensing justice, in quotation marks, misuse of uniforms and Mr. Moric would deploy forces in the liberated territory, according to the needs of the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, page 4. I'm not going to read out all the content. But if you follow the information. Brigade Biskic, who is the Deputy Chief of the military police administration - Mr. Lausic's deputy - outlined tasks before the start of combat operations, when they start, and when combat operations are completed, and the tasks that would be done. Page 5. General Lausic stated basic negative experiences in Flash concerning the military police, lack of vigour, failure to adapt, et cetera. And page 6, there is the record of what was discussed concerning persons entering the area. Mr. Moric dealing with preparations for entry and exit points of towns and proposing that he and General Lausic should meet once a day, exchange information, solve any problems. And he stated he, himself, had noticed the problem of lack of vigour in the actions of the police. And he comments upon assessments of the work of the military police, civilian police. And we've no need to go through the rest of the document, but turn to page 8 to see this record from the military police administration was sent to Mr. Moric, Mr. Djurica, Mr. Nad, chief of SIS. And if I can point out to the Court, to save time, that this information was reflected in Exhibit D41. The Court will remember I put to the Prosecution witness, Mr. Flynn, at that time, the record by the civilian police of this meeting, which is identical. So I don't propose to go into the two issues at the same time, because it would waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you understand that, Ms. Ozbolt, that there is an record here in another exhibit of the same matter?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the military police and the civilian police were preparing themselves for Operation Storm and how to deal with the security and control of law and order?
Yes, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning now to Exhibit P493, just to have a look at this document. It's dated the 3rd of August and is sent to the police administrations by Mr. Moric, ordering cooperation with the military police. You can see the kind of tasks that were being ordered. Again, this was an example of the military police and civil police planning to coordinate and work together; isn't that right?
This is the first time I see this document, but that was the intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this Court is aware of other orders that have been passed.
