In relation to Western Slavonia, where we looked at the first document showing by the order of the president that Mr. Moric and Mr. Lausic form a coordination committee with Dr. Majdak, they had the same responsibility, in relation to Operation Storm; isn't that right? That's the cooperation that we see happening here.
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that there is no equivalent order in relation to Operation Storm that we saw on the document dated the 6th of May, outlining the structure of the cooperation and coordination by the president or Chief of Staff?
There was no such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in view of the constraints of time, I am able to -- I take the view in relation to the answers of the witness, skip a substantial amount of documentation showing the coordination between Mr. Lausic and Mr. Moric from the 3rd of August onwards to the meeting in Plitvice. I don't know whether the Court would agree with that, or whether the Court would like me to go through those documents. They are all in evidence. I wouldn't be introducing anything -- no, I could read out the exhibit numbers, if that would be helpful to the Court to show the issues that are relevant to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, of course, this Chamber doesn't know what questions you would put to the witness in relation to those documents. If it is just to ask her whether she is aware of documents, and I leave it to that, or whether that is in accordance with her recollection. If it doesn't add much to the information, then I think it would be -- but I'm just looking at my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any specific questions, more than just drawing the attention of the witness to these documents, to see whether she has any other opinions about it, then, of course, the Chamber would be happy if you just say these and these are relevant documents in this context and leave it to that. If there's any document where have you doubt, you could just mention the nature of the document and ask the witness whether she has knowledge of the matter in such a way that it would add anything to what is already in that document. Of course, for the Chamber, it is guessing on what your questions would be. Therefore, if you consider that the content of the document is most important and that you do not expect the witness to add much to that, then the Chamber has no difficulties in accepting your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what I'll do, Your Honours is -- so that it's transparent, is to list the documents. I won't read them out now as that's probably tedious. And with the agreement of the Court, submit it to your learned clerk, and you now know the passage that was going to be gone through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are saying you are going to list them, that means that you describe what it is without going into the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Ms. Ozbolt, there would be -- if there is any document which you hear about, if you think that, first of all, you know the document; and second, that the content might be misleading or might not speak for itself, so you really have important matters to add to what you know to be the content of that document, then you're invited to ask Mr. Kay to stop for a moment. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will deal with it a very broad way, Ms. Ozbolt, rather than going through documents that are already in evidence. They are already exhibits in the case, and I have put them to witnesses previously on the same issue. Were you aware of a series of orders issued by Mr. Moric in relation to safety in the area, security in the area, and the prevention of crimes in the area, that he issued to the police administrations to stop crime.

I didn't see written orders. However, based on the reports that we received on all the steps taken by the Ministry of Interior, I knew that such orders had been issued, without seeing the texts of the orders themselves, since that was the internal matter of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. And that was the answer I would have expected if I had gone through each and every one. In relation to the military police and General Lausic, were you aware that in relation to the military police, he, likewise, issued such orders concerning safety, security, and prevention of crime to the battalions of the military police on regular occasions in August and September?
I can give you the same answer as before. On the basis of the information we received, that's something I knew. I didn't see their internal orders, nor was I supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that the two of them, in fact, were coordinating these measures together, in relation to crimes that were being committed, and they wanted their forces to stop?

They probably were coordinating their activities. I must admit, that I did not have any direct communications with either of them, since, as I told you already, I was engaged in other discussions concerning the Erdut Agreement at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to move to the last of the documents in this theme, which will be Exhibit D595. This is a record of a meeting held on the 15th of September, 1995. This document comes from the military police administration, but it's a meeting of the coordinative meeting with representatives of the MUP by the military police administration, held at Plitvice on the 15th of September - and a document that the Court is familiar with - and where the chiefs of police administration reported at this meeting with the military police administration what was happening in their area, and, likewise, the military police commanders did the same thing. First of all, were you aware that such a coordination meeting had taken place between the military police administration and Ministry of Interior, in relation to the law and order problems they were facing?
No, I wasn't. Perhaps somebody else in the office was. And I mean the office of the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In Western Slavonia, was that the similar coordination that was taking place after Operation Flash between Mr. Moric and Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't quite understand the question. Maybe I'm the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what we often do is to find out whether the witness understands the question. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit, that I don't, not fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kay, that is sufficient reason to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When we looked at the 6th of May, 1995, document, Exhibit D1484, and the president formed the coordination staff with Mr. -- Major-General Lausic, Mr. Moric, Dr. Majdak, and you described Western Slavonia as a situation with which you were involved, the meeting that we see took place on the 15th of September, after Storm, between the MUP and the military police. Was that a similar act of coordination from what you had experienced in Western Slavonia?

Let me be quite precise. I dealt with Western Slavonia until the commencement of Operation Flash. Thereafter, I received information about the situation on the ground. The coordination body you referred to, which was set up especially for Western Slavonia, was partly copied, as such, in the Knin area. The fact of the matter is that the two of them did cooperate, and as is clearly seen from the conclusions, they wanted to rectify their errors or any drawbacks that they observed in their activities in Western Slavonia, in order for these matters not to be repeated in their work in Sectors North and South. Let me repeat that I'm not privy to what happened afterwards because at the time, we were engage in the intensive negotiations for the Erdut Agreement that came to be signed two month the later. Therefore, I no longer followed the developments in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That deals with that matter and now moving on to some other smaller matters to ask you questions about. You worked in the president's office, and your immediate superior was who? Was it Mr. Sarinic?
It was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. During this period after Operation Storm, were you working in the president's office regularly? Were you there on a day-by-day basis?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of telephone calls made by General Cermak to president's office?
Depending on who he was calling. If he called the president, I did not necessarily have to know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if he called Mr. Sarinic?
I probably did know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he telephone the president's office, so far as you are aware, to let them know what was happening in Knin and the area from information he had received?
He probably did, and he probably spoke to them. I spoke to him on the issue involving the Serbs within the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just putting your conversation with him aside because we can go to that in a -- in a minute. In relation to the trouble and crime that was happening in the area down in the liberated territory, do you know if Mr. Cermak had telephoned in to let them know what was happening?
I don't have that sort of knowledge about when he called or who he spoke to, but he most probably did inform them of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to your matter of dealing with the people wanted for questioning and the criminal justice process in Croatia, was he finding out from you what was happening and how matters were going to develop?

To the best of my knowledge, I believed that I informed him of the discussions we had with Akashi and his team in Zagreb. Mr. Cermak was more frequently in touch with General Forand from the UN, who, on his part, had his communication channel with Mr. Akashi and the UN representatives in Zagreb. As for us, we communicated along this other line, with General Cermak and informed him of what the intended activities were, especially in relation to the issues discussed with Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were aware at the time that General Cermak was condemning crime that was happening publicly?
Yes. He appeared on television every day and presented his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what were those views?
He condemned what was happening and demanded that such matters be investigated into. I think that was the context in which he presented his views. It's hard to recall everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It been said in this court that he was part of a plan to drive out Serbs from the region and cause them to leave. Did he present himself to you as a man acting in that way?

No, absolutely not. First of all, there was no plan to drive out anyone. General Cermak is a highly tolerant person who I don't believe exhibited any sort of resentment or animosity toward anyone. I don't know him to be such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to a comment in your statement about him saying to you, I'm here because of you, because you persuaded me to take the job, is that an accurate scenario of what happened; or is that something that he said to you in a -- in a different context?

I was the minister of the justice from late 2003 up until early 2006. As such, as a minister charged with the justice system and penitentiaries, I visited Mr. Cermak and Mr. Markac in the UN detention unit here, and that was his first reaction upon seeing me here. I thought his reaction was an understandable one, because it was -- he was taken out of his own context of business and transferred to Knin, where he was supposed to exhibit all his skills, in terms of organisation and logistics; and one did not expect that the events would take the turn they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he saying that you persuaded him or that the office of which you were a member --

Well, the office where we worked included Sarinic and myself. In hindsight, I seem to realise that he was picked out of -- and dropped into something he -- where he could not expect what was to happen. We, ourselves, could not anticipate the developments that would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm pleased to say I think I have beaten the clock, and I'm able with the shortcut --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to finish earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That concludes my questioning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, we understand that the Markac Defence has no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will first have a break. And, Ms. Gustafson, you can start your cross-examination after the break. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, before I give you an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, I would like to clarify one thing with you, Ms. Ozbolt, and I'd like to have D1481 on the screen. Second page, please. Yes, I asked you about access to hearings, public hearings or not, and I am - I have to admit - a bit confused, because what I read is that you agree, in principle, I don't know what that adds in principle. But at least there's agreement with the presence of the UNCRO representatives at all court hearings which are in accordance with the positive legal acts of the Republike Hrvatske, public hearings and then the letter continues by saying: "Therefore, we agree with the monitoring of pre-trial investigation of persons who were processed for the severe criminal offences of terrorism and war crime." Now, is it public hearings? Then the "therefore" comes as a bit of a surprise, because I think it is common knowledge that most pre-trial proceedings are of a non-public character. I'm really confused by this letter, and if you can shed some light on it, then you are invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court hearings are public. Hearings held before a chamber are public. As for the proceedings held before an investigating judge, in each and every instance an application had to be made for their presence to be allowed at a hearing, at a questioning of someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, what everyone was entitled to see public hearings, UNCRO could watch that as well. If it was not public, it was, there was no automatic right to monitoring. Is that well understood? But that an application had to be made, and then the court would decide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We sent or, rather, the Ministry of Justice sent the UNCRO request for monitoring a certain court proceeding to the president of the court in question. The president would then grant such a request, and the proceedings could be followed from their commencement through to the end. The request that I forwarded to -- or, rather, this letter I forwarded it UNCRO representatives was not perhaps formulated in the best -- in the happiest of formulations. However, the practice was that with every request made by the international representatives to be present at court proceedings, every request was granted. And there were no difficulties encountered in their monitoring of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many such requests were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you how many such requests were made. At any rate, every request was granted. The monitoring of court proceedings did take place. At the time I was minister of the justice, and this is the case today, international representatives had been monitoring criminal proceedings taking place in Croatia, and there were no difficulties encountered in that quarter. I can't tell you the exact number, but it was the rule that every such request was granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're now talking not about the time when you were minister of justice, but you're now talking about late 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then I looked at the letter sent to you by Mr. Tomislav Penic. Do I understand that all those who were under investigation and who were in the UNCRO facility, were they all charged with offences for which the maximum penalty was ten years or higher; or were there any in that camp that were investigated for crimes not of such seriousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the crimes involved carried a sentence of more than ten years of imprisonment. The persons who were on the wanted list weren't charged with crimes incurring sentences exceeding ten years of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think so, you believe so. I'd like to -- it's your recollection that there was no one who was charged with any offence incurring a maximum penalty of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the general practice focussed on the crimes carrying a sentence of more than ten years. There would be no such insistence in respect of other less serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So for all of them there was compulsory defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, finally, that may be a detail, I wondered whether in D1480 where it reads: "If the accused is mute, death or incapable to defend himself," whether that should not be deaf instead of death. I can't check the original, but it surprised me. Then, Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Skare Ozbolt.
Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to start by asking you a couple of more specific questions on the evidence you gave yesterday about your proximity to President Tudjman and the frequency of the contact you had with him. And today you mentioned in a -- in answer to a question from Mr. Kay that if General Cermak had called President Tudjman, you wouldn't necessarily know about that. My question is: Is that the case generally, that, when people called the president directly, you wouldn't necessarily know about those phone calls or know what was said; is that right?

Well, my office was located on the same floor as that of the president. They were quite close one to another. But the president had his assistant, his head of office, and his entire specialist staff who knew who called him when. In other words, it was not my duty to know about that or any of the other assistants of who his were close to him, they didn't have to necessarily know of each and every instance of someone calling him or talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And similarly President Tudjman met frequently with his close advisors in one-on-one and small-group meetings, did he not, people like Mr. Sarinic, Mr. Radic, Minister Susak; is that right?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And President Tudjman didn't make it a habit or there was no systematic reporting to you of what happened in those one-on-one meetings with his close advisors, was there?
Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you say "of course," do you mean there was a systematic reporting to you of what happened at those meetings or there was not?

Look, I would have a briefing session with the president in the morning, which had to do with the general state of affairs which I briefed him on; I would occasionally see him during the day, whenever he sought me or I needed to inform of him of something; and then we would all meet at lunch-time to exchange information and coordinate our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And on that note your work was -- I think your evidence was that it was principally, in the beginning, in public relations and then in negotiations with the RSK and the UN. That was your sphere of work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, if we can get a time-frame because obviously that is not a complete area of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe it was public relations between 1991 to 1994 and then it changed to working as a representative in negotiations with the RSK and the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: From that point throughout 1995; is that right?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it's correct to say that you were not involved in matters relating to the function or operation of the Croatian army; is that right?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you weren't involved in the planning or implementation of military operations, were you?
That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you weren't present at military meetings when the planning of such operations took place, were you?
That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the Chamber has received evidence of a meeting for the planning of Operation Storm in late July. You weren't present at that meeting, were you?
At the meeting held where? Where exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It was a meeting on the 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I think the witness asked where it was held. I take it you want to refer to 31st of July, Brioni island. That's apparently what the witness would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you don't know what was discussed at that meeting or what plans were made at that meeting, do you?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move on to another topic, which is the Law on Temporary taking over and administration of property that you gave evidence about earlier. And I believe in your evidence you said that this law was a temporary measure, and I think you emphasised "temporary" to deal with the housing of refugees which was a big problem at the time?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, wasn't it --
That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- the case, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, that this law was intended by the Croatian leadership, including President Tudjman to permanently take Serb houses and settle Croats in them, in the Krajina area?

I will give you the following answer: It wasn't the intention to take these homes over. The intention was, and I believe I stated it quite clearly, that the Serb who did not wish to live in Croatia and who made that decision of their own accord and who wanted to sell their property could sell it on the market to whomever, or, that they could sell it to the Croatian government, which did buy such homes. The context I'm referring to is quite different from the one you formulated your question in. For that purpose, the agency for the sale of real estate was set up and was attached to the Government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're not aware of any statements by the leadership stating that this law was intended not as a temporary measure but to permanently settle Croats in houses that had previously belonged to Serbs; is that your evidence?

Can you please cite by way of example a statement which would be different? Only those homes in respect of which there was the wish to sell them were bought by the Republic of Croatia's government. Such a request had to be sent, the value of the homes had to be assessed, a price had to be negotiated, and, finally, the seller had to be paid his money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, the question put to you by Ms. Gustafson was, whether it was your evidence that you were not aware of any statement on permanence character rather than anything else. And you started your answer by saying, "Can you please cite by way of an example a statement ..." That is a counterquestion, and I would like to invite you not to respond questions by putting questions to Ms. Gustafson. Would you please keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Mr. President. All manner of statements were made. I don't know what it is exactly what Mrs. Prosecutor is referring to in putting the question to me, but I do know what the meaning of the law was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Her question was whether it is your evidence that you're not aware of any statement by the leadership. So if you are, if that's your evidence, please say, Yes; if you say, No, I know of some statement at any moment, please, tell Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall any such statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we please have P462 brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, this is a record of a meeting held on the 11th of August, 1995. And can you see from the cover page your name is listed as being present with the president. And can you see the names of the other participants of the meeting. Do you recall attending this meeting on the 11th of August with these participants?
If my name is there, then I probably did attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 14 in the English, and I believe page 24 in the B/C/S. Sorry, it should be the previous page in the B/C/S. Sorry, the page before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to Mr. Radic's statement. "President: Maybe something in connection with the issue you have mentioned at the beginning, the issue of Serbian houses, in quotation marks, we did not touch it, we just ignored it. "The Law on Property is in parliamentary procedure. However it has passed only the first reading and that things are not going smoothly in that regard. I think that we should, I have no idea in which way, but to solve that urgently." Do you recall Mr. Radic raising that issue at that meeting?
I have to say that I don't. It was a long time ago. But this is probably what he said. I'm not questioning this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page -- I'm sorry, two pages forward in the English, and I believe three pages forward in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We see Mr. Valentic. He was the prime minister; is that right?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He says: "President: In this law it is important that our people have security and that they cannot be thrown out, in my opinion, that is important, the wording because nobody will move in if they can be thrown out in a year. Now, the question is what form is most suitable to put this basic idea in?" Now, Mr. Valentic here is expressing the view that this should be a permanent transfer, that nobody should be thrown out in a year who's put into these houses; is that right?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then if you look at what Mr. Radic says immediately afterwards: "Nothing is more important than this. Nothing is more important in Croatia today than this, because people are coming, Croats. And I don't know. We don't have a report on this, but I don't know if you know that Vojnic used to have only 51 inhabitants. Today it is a town of 15.000 people. Tomorrow we can fill it up with 15.000. In addition, Lapac has 14 inhabitant, 14 Croats. Donji Lapac, 14 inhabitants. (It's more than the number of houses) I agree. But its strategically so important, and it's in such a position that we must repair the houses, Gojko, and put Croats there. Such is the position of the place." Now, Donji Lapac before the war was 99 percent Serb; is that right.
[In English] Almost.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Vojnic about 90 percent?
[Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And those municipalities are in the part of Croatia, in the central part of Croatia where it's the thinnest; is that right?
You mean the thinnest geographical speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when Mr. Radic says: "We must put Croats there, such is the position of the place," he is referring to the geography of those municipality, their geographical position, is he not?
Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go down to what the president says immediately after Mr. Radic. This is President Tudjman: "I am with the more radical. If someone has left the country and does not appear there, I don't know, a month, or three month, et cetera, that shall be considered, think of the wording, state property, et cetera. We have come out a war, et cetera, define it like that."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in the English, and I believe also in the B/C/S, the next speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VALENTIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Not three month, three months is too long, because we ... "The president: Okay a month then. "Mr. Radic: Then we must do it through a government decree, we can't wait." And then a little further down, Mr. Radic again: "Because the three-month deadline has already expired for Okucani and that's an area where we must then be able to move people in already." Now, Okucani is an area that was taken back as part of Operation Flash; is that right?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when Mr. Radic refers to the three-month deadline already expiring there, that's a reference to the fact that it's been over three months since Operation Flash; is that right?
Yes. That was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we continue, Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman says: "Yes, of course, people are coming and I don't know who says Rebic or somebody that they're going put them in camps. (Camps are out of the question)."

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK SAYS
utterances.text: "President, a thousand are coming from Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page. President Tudjman says: "Camps are out of the question, and, therefore, we must see about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADIC
utterances.text: "We have good houses, intact houses. Who do we keep them for? " A little further down the page, Vladimir Seks says: "President, we did put it into the law, for the second reading, but the people that move into a house have ownership security. They don't want temporary use. They must invest, repair, keep it in order, they want to own it." President Tudjman says: "Yes, well, that's clear. It's in our interests too ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, does the record of this meeting refresh your recollection about the intentions of the leadership to permanently resettle Croats in houses that had been abandoned by Serbs who had left the areas taken over in Operations Flash and Storm?

This took place in 1995, which was the time when Croatia, as far as the care for refugees and expellees was concerned, was pretty much on its knees. In the wake of operation, the areas that you have mentioned were completely vacant. People were constantly being expelled from Banja Luka, and they were arriving in Croatia. There was no accommodation available anymore for those people nor was there any possibility to expand the capacity. The only manner for them to provide them with shelter is to put them in houses, the abandoned houses. This is probably how this discussion went on and various views were expressed as well as various proposals. However, the final outcome was that the Law on Temporary Takeover of Property was adopted, and that the agency I mentioned earlier was set up for those who wished to sell their houses. In that way, the government solved the problem of ownership for those individuals who were inhabiting these houses on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We'll look at that law in a moment. But I'd just like to go back to one part of your answer, which was about these being empty spaces and Croatia being on its knees with a refugee problem. This wasn't just about refugees, was it? The intention of President Tudjman was to fill these empty spaces with Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, that was two questions. If we can just have one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The question would be: The intention of President Tudjman was to fill these empty spaces with Croats -- the question doesn't make sense if I don't talk about the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I mean, the refugee problem was not the issue. The issue was filling these spaces with Croats, wasn't it, for President Tudjman?

The contentious issue was where to place the Croats that were arriving from Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly from the area of Banja Luka. They had left their houses back there, and some of them were settled in these houses. The intention was not to put them up in those houses indefinitely but to provide them with a temporary shelter until conditions were ripe for them to return to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, just one observation. When we're talking about the intention, you put to the witness a document. It's about a certain discussion. It seems to me that what was the intention at what time or at least what was expressed as an intention at what time is repeatedly mixed up, because -- but please correct me when I'm wrong, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, one thing is what transpires from that discussion and another matter is what, then, happened later. Could we always clearly distinguish between what we are talking because it seems that Ms. Gustafson is asking questions about what -- what we see happening or what we read was said during this meeting; whereas, part of your answers seem to be about what the overall intention was whether or not expressed in that meeting, yes or no, and what the final result was. Let's try to keep things as clear as possible. If Ms. Gustafson asks about the meeting, let's look at what the meeting tell us. If Ms. Gustafson is asking about other moments or other meetings or other developments, let's always clearly define what we're talking about. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the guidance, Your Honour. If we could go to Exhibit P463; page 3 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. Sorry, if we could go to page 1 - sorry - to start, so the witness can see the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, this is a record of a meeting held on the 22nd of August, about ten days after the one we just looked at, between Mr. Radic and President Tudjman. Do you have any knowledge about this particular meeting?
No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go now to page 3 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. And at the bottom of page 3 in the English, and I believe in the middle of the page in B/C/S, if we could ... If we could just move down in the English. The B/C/S is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you see here Mr. Radic saying -- sorry, Dr. Radic. "It has been ruined very much. You have been to the main region only, but Drnis is the second biggest border town in Croatia. Vukovar first, then Drnis, 25.000 people. There was only 1.000 Serbs there. I'm talking about the town, I mean, the village as well. Everything around it has been ruined."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we just change the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in the English. Out the 25.000 maybe 5.000 could return and 20.000 can't. That's the situation in Drnis. The last paragraph he says: "So in my opinion, one third of 120.000 shall remain questionable, as for the remaining two thirds of 120." And then the last sentence he says: "However, our goal is to take them off the refugee status. The biggest problem is bringing people over there. I sat down and analysed it a bit ..." And then the president says -- If we can move down in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "Jure, regarding these returns we, as Croatia, should go for inviting people to come back and paying for their trips from Argentina, Australia, et cetera." If we can go to the next page in B/C/S. "We should organise some charter flights and ships and tell they will they could choose, give them houses, give them land, even take some kind of a poll on what they would be interested in. We have to offer them such a possibility, but the state should pay for that."

utterances.speaker: DR. RADIC SAYS
utterances.text: "It won't cost us a thing?" And the president says: "That would mean a thousand people and they would enter the Serb houses, et cetera." And Dr. Radic says: "Correct, correct. The space is empty."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I see that you now start reading the next paragraph. Mr. Kay did beat the clock. It seems that you're ignoring the clock a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was going to stop right there and ask one question and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do and we hear the answer, and then we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, this meeting is a reflection of President Tudjman's desire to fill those empty spaces with Croats, is it not?

This was a reflection of the situation that required these empty spaces to be filled in because, otherwise, they would pose a danger strategically speaking. This is it a very narrow area, facing the Republika Srpska, and if it is void of people, it was possible for the property to be demolished, incursions were possible to take place, and it was absolutely necessary to have people settle there. Since these were empty spaces, the houses were empty, and there were refugees all over the place, according to them, this was the only possible solution. When the president spoke about the idea of settling people from Argentina and from other countries all over the world, he probably referred to what subsequently happened, and that is, that people settled in the houses that were bought off. However, this particular idea relating to bringing people or, rather, Croats from all over the world was never put no practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for the day, Ms. Skare Ozbolt. We will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 5th of June, 9.00, in this same courtroom. I forgot to give you the same instructions as yesterday, that is not to speak with anyone about your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
